newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: South African liquor groups end dispute.
newsitem.headline: South African liquor groups end dispute.

text.p: South African wholesale liquor producers said on Wednesday they had resolved their dispute with the KWV co-operative over its plans to convert to a private company.
KWV, statutory regulator of the South African wine industry, was for many years the main exporter of the country's wine and brandy.
It sells in about 50 foreign countries but has plans to cut this number in a bid to serve fewer clients more efficiently.
In December KWV -- which has 4,400 wine-farmer members -- decided to convert to private company, raising fears that it would bring its financial muscle to bear in the domestic market.

Agriculture Minister Derek Hanekom brought a court action to halt the KWV plan, finding common cause with private companies such as Stellenbosch Farmers Winery (SFW), Distillers Corp Ltd, Douglas Green Bellingham, Gilbeys and Seagram grouped in the Cape Wine and Spirits Institute (CWSI).
Hanekom, who wants to see more blacks enter the wine industry, ordered an inquiry into it which recommended the scrapping of the Wine and Spirit Control Act under which KWV operates.
SFW director Andre Steyn told Reuters some people believed that if KWV converted to a company, the act would automatically fall away, but there was no legal certainty on the issue.
"(The KWV plan) held certain implications for us. We needed to have those implications clarified. A lot of emotion has surrounded the whole issue," he said.

"The basis of the fear was that KWV as a statutory body had acquired an asset base that it could then, as a company unfettered by any regulatory framework, utilise in an unfair way if it was allowed to compete with us directly," he said.
"Our suppliers would be their members, and then shareholders, in direct competition with us, and that's a very unhealthy situation."
Steyn said KWV had initially declined to discuss the CWSI's fears, but an agreement in principle was finally signed this week.
"All the concerns we had identified were placed on the table, negotiated and satisfactorily concluded with the KWV," he said.
Steyn said other CWSI concerns included KWV's supply of planting material, competition for grapes and wine, provision of information and "a whole variety of different aspects".
Sources close to the agreement who did not want to be identified said KWV had given the CWSI assurances that its marketing efforts would remain focused on exports, at least in the short term.

"All the infrastructure needed for KWV suddenly to have products -- lorries, distribution channels, marketing channels -- all these things cost an incredible amount of money if you start from scratch," one source said.
The sources said KWV believed its current activities were generating sufficient profits and that trying to break into the domestic market would not be attractive to the co-operative.
They said that because of a shortage of quality wine in South Africa, KWV did not even have enough products to service its foreign customers.

Hanekom's legal advisor Steven Goldblatt said the KWV-CWSI agreement should be probed by the competition board, because on the face of it the accord seemed "to fly in the face of a transparent, open and accessible market".
But Steyn said the CWSI fully intended to submit the agreement to the board.
"We will be inviting their comments. There is no hidden agenda or anything underhand about this whole thing," he said.

KWV's application to convert to a private company was due to have been heard in the Cape Town High Court on Wednesday but was postponed to April 2 to allow parties more time to study Hanekom's objections.
According to court papers, KWV has assets of more than one billion rand ($230 million) and no interest-bearing debts.
